doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Synthesizers and new technology
summary: Synthesizers failed to phrase like trombones and voices, but a sustained string pad worked well on the new CD.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Oh I was just talking about I guess the sound of your recordings and the technology. And sometimes I wonder when a new device comes out, whether it’s a digital reverb, or whether it’s synthesizers you know, digital synthesizers, if it becomes a tool to use, and sometimes that because it’s popular at that time maybe you over-use it and then later on you think that that’s not the way to go anymore.

Yeah, it happens. Like the syn drums, remember the syn drums? I used those for a while and then I stopped using them because they were being used so much. I think that on the whole things have gone forward recording-wise. I’m using synthesizers now. I used them on this last album, CD. I don’t use them quite the same as the younger artists use them. I’ve tried using them with my sound, you know that voice instrument sound that I became known for, and in that I would use like men singers with sometimes double unisons right with trombones and low saxes. Girls with double unisons with trumpets and higher saxophones. And I tried, hey I think I’ll embellish that, let’s try going a little further, let’s use a synthesizer with it as well. So we did a whole album once like that. I had about three or four synthesizers. I had one synthesizer was working with like the girl, brass, like a guy would play even single line things you know. I had three great keyboard guys on there, I remember I had Dick Hyman and I had oh God, I can’t think of the guys, but anyway three great jazz piano players and they’re all playing synthesizers. But anyway we found that we would double one synthesizer with the girls and trumpets, and one with the men and the trombones, and then another one was sustaining a pad like a string section would be. And we found that they couldn’t phrase. Like let’s take one of my old things like “Smoke Gets In Your Eyes.” It starts with trombones and men and they go, and low saxes, and they go [scats]. You know you can’t get that forte piano on the synthesizer. They go [scats]. So what you would hear, you’d hear the men and the trombones going [scats] and then you’d hear [scats] and they would keep going. And I’d say to the guy, can’t you use the pedal? They couldn’t do it.

It’s too hard. It could be done if they did that for a living, you know. So we discarded that completely because it wound up in the mixdown, I had to bring the synthesizer down so much that you wouldn’t hear that on the trombones and men or the girls and trumpets. But what we did find was the sustain pad of the string sound was really good. So we used that all the way, we used that quite a bit on “I Love Movies,” the new CD. And I do use that. And you know I’ve heard things that are done for movies and TV shows, the guys are doing it out in their garages, and they are great you know — big, big, big sounds and good sounds. So I think things on the whole have gone forward sound-wise. And I guess in that respect, yes it does change writing. The guys that are writing for synthesizers and doing those things in the garage, I don’t know, they might not even be writing the stuff
out. You know they might have it all up here, and might be sketching stuff and doing it all themselves in the garage you know.
Yeah. Because you can almost, of course they have devices now that you can play a part on a keyboard and it will be printed out in manuscript. So, amazing things out there nowadays.
